newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NZ's Birch sees further NZ dollar weakness this year.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Birch sees further NZ dollar weakness this year.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar was likely to extend its four U.S. cent fall of the last month over the rest of the year, New Zealand Finance Minister Bill Birch told Reuters on Monday.

Asked by Reuters after a Trans-Tasman Business Conference if he would be worried if the unit continued its recent fall Birch said: "I expect we will see it come down. They (the Reserve Bank of New Zealand) are foreshadowing further easings towards the end of this year so you are likely to get a little more easing."
The Kiwi dollar shed half a cent on the comments, falling to a low of US$0.6437 after a closing local trading at US$0.6482.
The New Zealand dollar has fallen sharply in past few weeks following a period in which it has been perceived by market commentators as over-valued.

Ahead of the New Zealand Budget and Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) monetary policy statement on June 26 and June 27 respectively, the New Zealand dollar had been trading around U$0.6900 for a five month period.
Birch said he was more comfortable with the currency at its current levels than where it was last week.
"From the point of view of the mix between interest rates and exchange rates, the rebalancing has been very positive, I think, in terms of long term growth," Birch said.
The RBNZ targets a monetary conditions index (MCI), a measure derived from the exchange rate and short term interest rates.

In its June statement the RBNZ assumed the index at 825, and allowed a fifty point copmfort zone either side on this level. The recent sharp decline in the dollar has led the markets to raise short term rates to keep the MCI within the target band.
Birch said the lower exchange rate would aid exports and an export-led recovery would give New Zealand a much longer growth cycle.
"You don't want interest rates so low that you are going to cause a burst of investment that might be speculative or drive up tradesmens' wages as house prices rise."
"That caused quite a lot of pressure on our economy last time round," he said.
New Zealand exporters were in a strong position to bounce back quickly after the recent fall in the currency, Birch said.
"They have actually been through a couple of years of pretty hard times and they've maintained thier export levels - they've captured efficiencies during that period," he said.
Birch earlier told a Trans-Tasman Business Circle luncheon that the New Zealand government would place higher emphasis on improving access for its exporters to international markets.
Birch said he had spoken with Australian Treasurer, Peter Costello, about Trans-Tasman taxation and approval required on investment between Australia and New Zealand.

"Most Australian businesses would say they were confident of getting approval to invest in New Zealand, or the other way around, but there is a pretty big cost in the delay for those approvals," Birch said.
The next step to improve this process was to discuss possible changes in the present arrangements with business, he said.
